claims.text: A hybrid high-throughput CALPHAD and machine-learning methodology can accurately predict melting temperatures for refractory high-entropy alloys.
The hybrid methodology can accurately predict entropy of fusion for refractory high-entropy alloys.
Standard thermodynamic databases are incomplete or inaccurate for high-temperature, multicomponent alloy systems.
Lennard-Jones potentials alone cannot provide reliable structural predictions for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Refractory Nb-Mo-Ta-W-V-type alloys have sparse melting-property data because their melting temperatures exceed 1800 °C and relevant phase diagrams are lacking.
High-throughput CALPHAD can screen thousands of compositions at 5 at.% increments and evaluate phases at Tm, 0.8Tm, and 0.5Tm.
A machine-learning model based on Holder means of elemental properties can correct CALPHAD predictions for lattice distortion and database inaccuracies.
Machine-learning models trained on ordered-compound data and using elemental and structural descriptors can predict elastic moduli of a disordered NbTaTiV refractory HEA with relatively low error.
Lattice distortion produces deviations from ideal solid-solution behavior that standard CALPHAD databases fail to capture accurately.
Experimental validation above 1800 °C is impossible when available equipment cannot reach the required temperature.
The lack of HEA phase diagrams limits the thermodynamic data available for phase-formation prediction.
Extrapolating structural properties from ordered compounds to disordered HEAs bridges sparse experimental data to accurate melting-property predictions.
The hybrid method will identify compositions with melting temperatures above 1250 °C and targeted BCC/L21 phase fractions.
The hybrid method's melting-property predictions will have accuracy comparable to experimental data.
Standard CALPHAD or Lennard-Jones molecular dynamics will exhibit errors exceeding 15% in elastic moduli or predict incorrect phase stability.
The method is valid for disordered solid-solution alloys governed by high-entropy theory but excludes oxides, carbides, and nitrides with very large heats of formation.
Ordered-compound training data can reasonably extrapolate to disordered refractory HEAs under suitable conditions.
Prediction accuracy remains highly dependent on the quality of the underlying thermodynamic database.
Missing or erroneous binary interaction parameters can make predictions unreliable, and the proposed machine-learning correction may not fully compensate.
